title: Bennet, Young, Colleagues Reintroduce Bipartisan PASTEUR Act to Fight Antimicrobial Resistance
date_evidence: meta property=article:published_time content=2026-06-24T14:55:41+00:00 ; Jun 24, 2026 | Press Releases
key_claim: A bipartisan group of five US senators reintroduced the PASTEUR Act on 24 June 2026, which would establish a Federal Subscription Model paying developers of eligible antibiotics and antifungals annual contract values of $75 million to $300 million per year, with terms up to 10 years, delinked from sales volume; more than 2.8 million antibiotic-resistant infections occur in the US each year causing over 35,000 deaths, the cost of treating the most common multidrug-resistant infections exceeds $4.6 billion annually, many innovative antibiotic companies have filed for bankruptcy, and the bill was first introduced in September 2020 but has never received a floor vote.
frame_summary: A US Senate bill reintroduction frames the antibiotic market as a structural failure that a delinked subscription payment model is designed to fix, signalling renewed bipartisan momentum behind pull incentives.
notes: Tier 1 US Senate press release reintroducing the PASTEUR Act on 24 June 2026. (Page 403-blocks the audit fetcher; figures confirmed via WebFetch on 2026-06-28.)

title: Economic reform can save antibiotic innovation (Nature Outlook: Antimicrobial resistance)
key_claim: The pipeline of antibiotics has been reduced to a trickle; the UK NHS subscription pilot paying a fixed annual fee for access regardless of volume is now open to other drug manufacturers; an analysis estimated the G7 and EU should collectively contribute about $363 million annually over ten years to fund the pull incentives needed to create one antibiotic, and the Office of Health Economics estimated in 2022 that if G7 and EU countries implemented pull incentives they would make back between 11 and 28 times the cost over a 30-year period, mostly in health-care savings; the US House reintroduced the PASTEUR Act in February with contracts of $75 million to $300 million per year, the EU Parliament proposed transferable data-exclusivity vouchers, and Canada, Sweden and Japan have developed pull-incentive programmes.
frame_summary: A Nature Outlook analysis argues the antibiotic market is structurally broken and that governments across the G7 and EU are now building pull-incentive programmes, though the funding remains below the level needed.
notes: Tier 2 Nature Outlook. Author Gareth Morgan is an industry executive (Shionogi/Qpex); content is factual synthesis of the international pull-incentive landscape, treated as institutional analysis.

title: Six key developments in the fight against antimicrobial resistance (Nature Outlook)
key_claim: Recent science is producing antibiotic candidates: researchers at MIT used two generative-AI algorithms that generated 29 million compounds with predicted antibacterial activity, shortlisting 90 and synthesising 24, one of which (DN1) cleared methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus skin infections in mice; the oral gonorrhoea antibiotic zoliflodacin was approved in the US in December and a natural-product intermediate (premethylenomycin C lactone) was found to be up to 500 times more potent than a known antibiotic against several Gram-positive bacteria.
frame_summary: A Nature Outlook round-up shows the antibacterial discovery pipeline is generating genuinely novel candidates, indicating the bottleneck is commercialisation economics rather than science.
notes: Tier 2 Nature Outlook. Used to evidence that scientific discovery is advancing while the market lags.

publisher: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE)
title: A new model for evaluating and purchasing antimicrobials in the UK
date_evidence: Evergreen NICE life-sciences programme page describing the antimicrobial subscription model; accessed 28 June 2026
key_claim: NICE and NHS England developed a subscription-style payment model that pays companies a fixed annual fee for antimicrobials based on a health technology assessment of their value rather than on the volume used; the project delivered a global first in July 2022 by awarding subscription-style contracts (for cefiderocol and ceftazidime with avibactam) in which payments are delinked from volume, and the model is now being scaled to more antimicrobials across the UK; AMR causes around 700,000 deaths each year globally, predicted to rise to 10 million by 2050 if no action is taken.
frame_summary: The UK regulator describes the world's first delinked, value-based subscription model for antibiotics, now being scaled, as the template other countries are following.
notes: Tier 1 evergreen programme page. Source of the UK model mechanics and the AMR Review headline burden figures.

title: Antimicrobial resistance (fact sheet)
date_evidence: Evergreen WHO fact sheet on antimicrobial resistance; accessed 28 June 2026
key_claim: WHO estimates bacterial AMR was directly responsible for 1.27 million global deaths in 2019 and contributed to 4.95 million deaths; the World Bank estimates AMR could result in $1 trillion additional healthcare costs by 2050 and $1 trillion to $3.4 trillion in GDP losses per year by 2030; the clinical pipeline of new antimicrobials is almost dry, with WHO's review identifying 27 antibiotics in clinical development that address priority pathogens, of which only 6 were classified as innovative.
frame_summary: WHO frames AMR as a top global health and economic threat sitting alongside a near-empty antibiotic pipeline and an access-and-innovation crisis.
notes: Tier 1 evergreen fact sheet. Source of global burden, economic-cost and pipeline-scarcity figures.

title: EU Council Publishes Final 2026 Pharma Package: New Regulatory Framework for Medicinal Products
key_claim: The Council of the European Union published the final compromise texts of the 2026 Pharma Package on 6 March 2026, the EU's most significant pharmaceutical overhaul in over two decades; it introduces a novel transferable exclusivity voucher for priority antimicrobials granting 1 additional year of data protection that can be applied to another product, with a blockbuster clause barring use on products exceeding 490 million euros in prior four-year sales; the European Parliament's public-health committee approved the trilogue on 18 March 2026, with final adoption by Parliament and Council slated for autumn 2026.
frame_summary: Trade reporting confirms the EU has written a transferable exclusivity voucher for priority antimicrobials into its adopted pharma-package texts, formalising a pull incentive at EU level.
notes: Tier 3 trade press reporting the EU Council's 6 March 2026 texts; article itself published 8 April 2026, in-window.

title: AMR Action Fund
date_evidence: Evergreen IFPMA initiative page for the AMR Action Fund (last modified 2026-06-25); accessed 28 June 2026
key_claim: The industry-led AMR Action Fund is a USD 1 billion initiative, backed by 23 pharmaceutical companies from Europe, the US and Japan, that aims to bring 2-4 new antibiotics to patients by 2030 and has made over 10 investments; it states that while the Fund helps bridge the clinical funding gap it cannot address the fundamental problem that not enough antibiotics are being produced, and that market-based policy reforms including reimbursement reform and new incentives are required to create sustainable market conditions.
frame_summary: The largest industry antibiotic fund argues that private capital alone cannot fix the market and that government pull incentives and reimbursement reform are indispensable.
